---
title: "xenium_nb — clustering"
subtitle: "Per-sample Leiden resolution sweep, QC, and clusters in tissue"
# Pin the kernel by name, as plot_follicle.qmd does. Apptainer bind-mounts $HOME, so
# kernelspecs from ~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels shadow the container's own — quarto's
# default "python3" then resolves to a host env missing the pipeline's packages, and
# every cell fails at import under `error: true` while the render still exits 0.
jupyter: python_spatial
format:
  pptx:
    reference-doc: ouhsc_ppt_template.pptx
    # `#` becomes a Section Header slide, `##` a Title-and-Content slide. Without
    # this pandoc infers the level from the headings present, so adding the first
    # `#` would silently demote every `##` to a bullet.
    slide-level: 2
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  # Keep rendering when a cell raises. The per-sample sections come from one loop over
  # the staged zarrs, so a missing sample is simply absent rather than an error — but a
  # sample whose plots raise would otherwise take the whole deck down with it. The cost
  # is that a genuinely broken cell yields an error slide and an exit code of 0 — read
  # the slides, not just the exit status.
  error: true
---

```{python}
# | tags: [setup]
from pathlib import Path

import anndata as ad
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import zarr
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm, Normalize

# The reference template is 16:9 at 10 x 5.625in; leave room for a slide title.
FIGSIZE = (9.0, 4.3)
# Inches reserved beside the in-tissue plots for their cluster legend, which sits
# outside the axes and would otherwise be cropped by tight_layout.
LEGEND_WIDTH = 1.4
# Fraction of the in-tissue axes the cell dots should cover, which sets their size.
SPATIAL_COVERAGE = 0.45

# Every clustered zarr is staged into this notebook's working directory by the Nextflow
# process, so globbing is the whole input contract — no params to pass or drift. These
# are cluster_sdata's zarrs, not create_sdata's: they carry X_umap and the leiden_res_*
# columns, and their cells are already past the min_counts cut.
ZARRS = sorted(Path(".").glob("*.zarr"))
if not ZARRS:
    raise FileNotFoundError("No .zarr directories staged next to the notebook.")

# Cap the panels per row so a wide sweep wraps instead of shrinking to nothing.
MAX_COLS = 3

# The sweep is split across this many slides per sample so ten resolutions do not shrink
# to ten unreadable thumbnails on one slide. Bump to 3 for a wider sweep — the per-sample
# loop below iterates range(CLUSTER_SLIDES), so nothing else needs editing.
CLUSTER_SLIDES = 2

# The spatial and H&E slides show one resolution, not the sweep — overlaying ten
# panels on tissue would be unreadable and the point of those slides is whether a
# cluster is a coherent structure, not where to cut the sweep. Nearest available
# resolution wins, so a run with a custom --resolutions still renders.
#
# 0.5 rather than the 1.0 this was set to before the clustering recipe changed. That
# value was chosen when the old recipe needed high resolution to resolve anything: it
# gave 8 clusters at r=1.0 on a 21k-cell test ROI. The current recipe resolves far more
# per unit resolution, and cluster count also grows with cell count, so on a whole slide
# r=1.0 produces a count this slide cannot show legibly — it is a single dense
# full-tissue plot, and past ~10 clusters the palette falls back to tab20's dark/light
# pairs, where adjacent structures stop being distinguishable at plot scale.
#
# It is a legibility choice, not a claim about the right resolution. That judgement is
# made by reading the sweep slides, and recorded per sample in sample_summary's
# chosen_resolutions.csv — which this deck deliberately does not read, since it is the
# deck the judgement is made FROM.
SPATIAL_RESOLUTION = 0.5

def load_sample(path):
    """Read one zarr's obs, UMAP, and spatial coords without pulling X into memory.

    ad.io.read_elem on the table's zarr groups reads obs/obsm only — the count matrix
    stays on disk. That matters more here than for an h5ad cohort: spatialdata.read_zarr
    would also materialize every image and the full X for each sample at once.
    """
    store = zarr.open(f"{path}/tables/table", mode="r")
    df = ad.io.read_elem(store["obs"])
    umap = ad.io.read_elem(store["obsm"]["X_umap"])
    df["umap_1"] = umap[:, 0]
    df["umap_2"] = umap[:, 1]
    spatial = ad.io.read_elem(store["obsm"]["spatial"])
    df["spatial_x"] = spatial[:, 0]
    df["spatial_y"] = spatial[:, 1]

    # This deck computes no QC metric of its own. Every column it plots — including
    # pct_control, which it used to derive here — comes from create_sdata, which
    # annotates them at the one point X and the reader's own columns are together in
    # memory. A report that recomputes a metric is a second definition of it, and the
    # two drift silently.
    #
    # Deliberately no fallback for zarrs written before create_sdata emitted a column:
    # a fallback is that second definition wearing a disguise, and it would let a stale
    # cohort render a deck whose numbers came from somewhere other than the pipeline.
    # Failing here instead names the fix, which is to re-run create_sdata.
    missing = [c for c, _, _ in QC_METRICS if c not in df.columns]
    if missing:
        raise KeyError(
            f"{Path(path).name}: obs is missing {missing}. These come from create_sdata "
            "— re-run it over this sample rather than deriving them here."
        )

    return df


def resolution_columns(df):
    """The sweep's leiden columns, ordered by resolution rather than by string.

    Discovered from obs rather than hardcoded: --resolutions is a pipeline param, so the
    set of columns is whatever the run that produced these zarrs chose. Sorting on the
    float matters — a plain sort puts leiden_res_1.00 before leiden_res_0.20.
    """
    cols = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith("leiden_res_")]
    return sorted(cols, key=lambda c: float(c.removeprefix("leiden_res_")))


def resolution_parts(res_cols, nparts):
    """Split the ordered sweep into nparts balanced, contiguous groups — one slide each.

    A wide sweep (the default 0.1-1.0 is ten resolutions) crammed onto one slide shrinks
    every UMAP to an unreadable thumbnail, and choosing a resolution is exactly what this
    slide is for. Splitting across slides keeps the panels legible; the groups are
    contiguous so each slide still reads low-to-high. np.array_split balances the
    remainder (ten -> 5+5, seven -> 4+3) instead of stranding one panel alone on a slide.
    """
    return [list(part) for part in np.array_split(res_cols, nparts)]


def spatial_column(df):
    """The sweep column closest to SPATIAL_RESOLUTION, for the in-tissue slides."""
    cols = resolution_columns(df)
    if not cols:
        raise ValueError("No leiden_res_* columns in obs — was this zarr clustered?")
    return min(cols, key=lambda c: abs(float(c.removeprefix("leiden_res_")) - SPATIAL_RESOLUTION))


def panel_grid(n, figsize=FIGSIZE):
    """A balanced grid sized to exactly n panels, with any leftover axes removed.

    Rows first, then columns back-solved from the row count, so the panels spread evenly
    instead of filling rows to MAX_COLS and stranding a remainder: 4 metrics land 2x2
    rather than 3 across with one alone under a two-thirds gap. 6 still lands 2x3.

    delaxes, not set_visible(False): a hidden axes still reserves its cell under
    tight_layout, which squeezes the real panels into a fraction of the slide and
    strands the labels. Removing it reclaims the space.
    """
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / MAX_COLS))
    ncols = int(np.ceil(n / nrows))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=figsize, squeeze=False)
    flat = axes.ravel()
    for ax in flat[n:]:
        fig.delaxes(ax)
    return fig, flat[:n]


def point_size(ax, n_cells, coverage):
    """Marker area (pt²) that lets n_cells cover `coverage` of these axes, once.

    A fixed size cannot serve every tissue plot: at s=3 a 21k-cell strip reads well but a
    32k-cell section is a solid mat of dots, and at s=1 the strip is speckle. The same
    sample also needs a smaller dot in a five-panel sweep than on a full-slide plot.
    Taking the axes' own area covers both — get_position() is the pre-tight_layout
    fraction of the figure, close enough for a marker size. 72 pt to the inch, squared,
    converts inches² to the pt² units scatter's `s` is in.
    """
    w, h = ax.get_figure().get_size_inches()
    pos = ax.get_position()
    area_pt2 = (pos.width * w) * (pos.height * h) * 72 ** 2
    return float(np.clip(coverage * area_pt2 / n_cells, 0.5, 6.0))


def tissue_grid(x0, x1, y0, y1):
    """A single-axes figure shaped like the tissue it will hold, plus room for a legend.

    A fixed FIGSIZE wastes the slide on anything that is not 2:1: a tall section renders
    as a sliver down the middle of a wide figure, because set_aspect("equal") is
    non-negotiable for tissue. Sizing the figure to the data's aspect instead means the
    image pandoc embeds is all tissue, and PowerPoint centres it on the slide.
    """
    aspect = (x1 - x0) / (y1 - y0)
    plot_w = FIGSIZE[0] - LEGEND_WIDTH
    if aspect >= plot_w / FIGSIZE[1]:
        w, h = plot_w, plot_w / aspect
    else:
        w, h = FIGSIZE[1] * aspect, FIGSIZE[1]
    return plt.subplots(figsize=(w + LEGEND_WIDTH, h))


def style_tissue(ax, col, legend=True):
    """Shared framing for the in-tissue plots: square units, no frame, optional legend.

    A legend, not the on-data labels the UMAP slides use: clusters are spatially
    interleaved, so a label at a cluster's median centroid routinely lands inside a
    different cluster. The sweep panels pass legend=False — one legend per panel would
    cost more width than the tissue itself, and their titles carry the cluster count.
    """
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.spines[["top", "right", "bottom", "left"]].set_visible(False)
    if legend:
        ax.legend(
            loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5), frameon=False,
            fontsize=6, markerscale=6, ncols=2,
            title=f"resolution {col.removeprefix('leiden_res_')}", title_fontsize=6,
        )


def style_umap(ax, title):
    """UMAP axes carry no interpretable units — drop the frame, keep the title."""
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8, loc="left")
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.spines[["top", "right", "bottom", "left"]].set_visible(False)


def cluster_colors(labels):
    """(ordered levels, level -> colour) for one cluster column.

    Numeric order so a cluster keeps its colour across every slide showing the same
    resolution, and so the on-data labels read in order.

    tab10 below 11 clusters, tab20 above: tab20 is ten dark/light *pairs*, so a
    2-cluster panel drawn from it is navy against pale blue — nearly invisible at
    sweep-panel size, which is exactly where the low resolutions land. tab10's first
    two are blue and orange. Past 20 the palette cycles, which the on-data labels on
    the UMAP panels compensate for.
    """
    levels = sorted(labels.unique(), key=int)
    cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab10" if len(levels) <= 10 else "tab20")
    return levels, {level: cmap(i % cmap.N) for i, level in enumerate(levels)}


# (column, panel title, log colour scale). Counts span orders of magnitude, so a linear
# ramp puts almost every cell in the bottom colour; the rest are bounded. No mito or
# doublet panel: the Xenium panel carries no MT- genes at all, so pct_counts_mt would
# read 0.0 for every cell, and no doublet caller runs in this pipeline.
# Upper quantile the QC-on-UMAP colour ramps are clipped at.
#
# Without it these panels are unreadable. Left unclipped, matplotlib scales to the
# observed maximum, which on every one of these metrics is a far outlier: cell area ran
# to 1,600 µm² against a median of 45, so the whole ramp compressed into its bottom
# thirtieth and the panel rendered as a uniform dark square. Genes-detected and
# negative-control were the same. Only the log-scaled panel survived, because log
# compresses the tail on its own.
#
# The point of these panels is finding a REGION of the manifold that runs high, so the
# cells beyond the clip are exactly the ones whose value does not need resolving — they
# saturate, and the ramp spends its range where the reading is made. qc_report clips its
# equivalent scatters the same way, at fixed 150/80; a quantile is used here instead so
# it holds across samples of different depth without per-sample constants.
QC_CLIP_QUANTILE = 0.99

QC_METRICS = [
    ("transcript_counts", "Transcripts", True),
    # n_genes_by_transcripts, not n_genes_by_counts: the latter existed only because
    # cluster_sdata* re-ran calculate_qc_metrics with the default expr_type. That call
    # is gone, and create_sdata's own column — computed once, before any filtering — is
    # what clustered zarrs now carry.
    ("n_genes_by_transcripts", "Genes detected", False),
    ("cell_area", "Cell area (µm²)", False),
    ("pct_control", "Negative control %", False),
]


def qc_umap(sample):
    """One slide's figure: this sample's UMAP, once per QC metric.

    A continuous viridis ramp: every cell here is already past cluster_sdata's
    min_counts cut, so the question is not where to put a threshold but whether a region
    of the manifold runs high — a magnitude read, which a ramp answers.

    Debris is what to look for. The negative-control panel is the Xenium-specific one:
    a cluster that lights up there is reading control probes, not biology, and should be
    dropped rather than annotated.
    """
    d = samples[sample]
    metrics = [(c, t, log_c) for c, t, log_c in QC_METRICS if c in d.columns]
    fig, axes = panel_grid(len(metrics))

    for ax, (metric, title, log_c) in zip(axes, metrics):
        values = d[metric]
        # Clip the top of the ramp so the panel resolves the range the reading is made
        # in — see QC_CLIP_QUANTILE. Fall back to the maximum if the quantile is not
        # above the floor, which happens when a metric is near-constant (pct_control is
        # 0 for most cells on a clean sample) and would otherwise give an invalid norm.
        vmax = float(values.quantile(QC_CLIP_QUANTILE))
        if log_c:
            vmin = max(values[values > 0].min(), 1e-9)
            # Guard the log norm: a zero or negative would raise, and transcript_counts
            # can be small on debris.
            norm = LogNorm(vmin=vmin, vmax=max(vmax, vmin * 1.000001))
        else:
            vmin = float(values.min())
            norm = Normalize(vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax if vmax > vmin else float(values.max()))
        scatter = ax.scatter(
            d["umap_1"], d["umap_2"], c=values,
            cmap="viridis", norm=norm,
            # Opaque: a colorbar inherits its mappable's alpha and would draw the ramp
            # blended toward white.
            s=2, alpha=1.0, edgecolors="none", rasterized=True,
        )
        # Say the panel is clipped, so a saturated region is not read as a plateau.
        clipped = (values > vmax).sum()
        style_umap(ax, f"{title} · {clipped:,} above p{QC_CLIP_QUANTILE * 100:g}"
                   if clipped else title)
        cbar = fig.colorbar(scatter, ax=ax, fraction=0.045, pad=0.02)
        cbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=6)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {len(d):,} cells", fontsize=9, x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def cluster_umap(sample, part):
    """One slide's figure: this sample's UMAP for part `part` of the resolution sweep.

    The point of the slide is choosing a resolution, so the panels are the sweep and the
    titles carry the cluster count. The sweep is split into CLUSTER_SLIDES contiguous
    slides (part is 0-based) so each slide shows a legible handful of panels rather than
    the whole sweep at thumbnail size.

    Labels are drawn on the clusters rather than in a legend: at 25 clusters a legend
    would eat the panel, and tab20 has to cycle anyway — the on-data label is what
    actually identifies a cluster, so colour only has to separate neighbours.
    """
    d = samples[sample]
    res_cols = resolution_columns(d)
    if not res_cols:
        raise ValueError(f"{sample}: no leiden_res_* columns in obs — was this zarr clustered?")
    cols = resolution_parts(res_cols, CLUSTER_SLIDES)[part]

    fig, axes = panel_grid(len(cols))

    for ax, col in zip(axes, cols):
        labels = d[col].astype(str)
        levels, colors = cluster_colors(labels)
        for level in levels:
            m = labels == level
            ax.scatter(
                d.loc[m, "umap_1"], d.loc[m, "umap_2"],
                color=colors[level],
                s=2, alpha=1.0, edgecolors="none", rasterized=True,
            )
            # Median, not mean: a cluster with a stray arm would drag the mean off the
            # cells it is labelling.
            ax.annotate(
                level,
                (d.loc[m, "umap_1"].median(), d.loc[m, "umap_2"].median()),
                fontsize=5, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center",
                color="black",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", facecolor="white",
                          alpha=0.7, edgecolor="none"),
            )
        style_umap(ax, f"resolution {col.removeprefix('leiden_res_')} · {len(levels)} clusters")

    # Name the resolution span on the title so the slides are self-identifying.
    span = f"{cols[0].removeprefix('leiden_res_')}–{cols[-1].removeprefix('leiden_res_')}"
    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {len(d):,} cells · resolutions {span}", fontsize=9, x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def spatial_clusters(sample):
    """One slide's figure: this sample's cells in tissue coordinates, coloured by cluster.

    The UMAP says which cells group together; only this says whether that group is a
    structure. Centroids from obsm["spatial"], not cell_boundaries polygons — at
    whole-section scale a 15 µm cell is well under a pixel, so the polygons cost a great
    deal of render time to draw the same dots.

    y is inverted because Xenium global coordinates run downward from the top-left of
    the slide image; without it the tissue renders upside down relative to the scan.
    """
    d = samples[sample]
    col = spatial_column(d)
    labels = d[col].astype(str)
    levels, colors = cluster_colors(labels)

    fig, ax = tissue_grid(
        d["spatial_x"].min(), d["spatial_x"].max(),
        d["spatial_y"].min(), d["spatial_y"].max(),
    )
    size = point_size(ax, len(d), SPATIAL_COVERAGE)
    for level in levels:
        m = labels == level
        ax.scatter(
            d.loc[m, "spatial_x"], d.loc[m, "spatial_y"],
            color=colors[level], label=level,
            s=size, alpha=1.0, edgecolors="none", rasterized=True,
        )

    ax.invert_yaxis()
    style_tissue(ax, col)
    fig.suptitle(
        f"{sample} · {len(d):,} cells · resolution {col.removeprefix('leiden_res_')}"
        f" · {len(levels)} clusters",
        fontsize=9, x=0.01, ha="left",
    )
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def spatial_sweep(sample, part):
    """One slide's figure: the tissue once per resolution in part `part` of the sweep.

    The UMAP sweep answers which resolutions split which blobs; this answers which of
    those splits are spatial. A resolution that carves a UMAP blob in two but scatters
    both halves through the same tissue is splitting on depth or noise, and that only
    shows up side by side like this.

    Same CLUSTER_SLIDES split as the UMAP sweep, so slide n here holds the same
    resolutions as slide n there and the two can be read against each other.
    """
    d = samples[sample]
    res_cols = resolution_columns(d)
    if not res_cols:
        raise ValueError(f"{sample}: no leiden_res_* columns in obs — was this zarr clustered?")
    cols = resolution_parts(res_cols, CLUSTER_SLIDES)[part]

    fig, axes = panel_grid(len(cols))

    for ax, col in zip(axes, cols):
        labels = d[col].astype(str)
        levels, colors = cluster_colors(labels)
        size = point_size(ax, len(d), SPATIAL_COVERAGE)
        for level in levels:
            m = labels == level
            ax.scatter(
                d.loc[m, "spatial_x"], d.loc[m, "spatial_y"],
                color=colors[level],
                s=size, alpha=1.0, edgecolors="none", rasterized=True,
            )
        ax.invert_yaxis()
        style_tissue(ax, col, legend=False)
        ax.set_title(
            f"resolution {col.removeprefix('leiden_res_')} · {len(levels)} clusters",
            fontsize=8, loc="left",
        )

    span = f"{cols[0].removeprefix('leiden_res_')}–{cols[-1].removeprefix('leiden_res_')}"
    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {len(d):,} cells · resolutions {span}", fontsize=9, x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def md_table(df):
    """Render a DataFrame as a markdown table.

    Built by hand rather than via df.style (HTML-only, renders as nothing in pptx) or
    df.to_markdown (needs tabulate, which the container does not carry).
    """
    header = "| " + " | ".join(str(c) for c in df.columns) + " |"
    rule = "| " + " | ".join("---" for _ in df.columns) + " |"
    rows = ["| " + " | ".join(str(v) for v in row) + " |" for row in df.itertuples(index=False)]
    display(Markdown("\n".join([header, rule] + rows)))


samples = {}
for path in ZARRS:
    df = load_sample(path)
    # obs["sample"] is written by create_sdata and survives clustering, so the section
    # headings carry the sample's own id rather than whatever the zarr got named.
    name = df["sample"].iloc[0]
    samples[name] = df

sample_order = sorted(samples)
```

## Clusters per resolution

```{python}
# One row per sample, one column per resolution: the cluster counts the per-sample
# slides show one at a time, in the one place they can be compared. Not hardcoded —
# it iterates sample_order, so it picks up samples with no edit here.
res_cols = resolution_columns(samples[sample_order[0]])
rows = []
for s in sample_order:
    d = samples[s]
    row = {"sample": s, "cells": f"{len(d):,}"}
    for col in res_cols:
        row[col.removeprefix("leiden_res_")] = d[col].nunique()
    rows.append(row)
md_table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

```{python}
# One `# <sample>` section per sample, driven by sample_order rather than a hardcoded
# block each. The cohort changes — samples are added and dropped — and a hardcoded list
# silently omits a new sample while raising KeyError on a removed one.
#
# The headings are emitted with display(Markdown(...)) from inside an ordinary cell, NOT
# under `output: asis`. Under asis an inline figure lands between the markdown blocks and
# leaves the *next* heading not starting its own line, so pandoc emits a literal "## ..."
# as text and drops the image. display(Markdown) does not hit it: each call emits its own
# complete block, and the plot functions end with plt.show() so the figure lands between
# them.
for s in sample_order:
    display(Markdown(f"# {s}"))

    display(Markdown("## QC metrics on the UMAP"))
    qc_umap(s)

    for part in range(CLUSTER_SLIDES):
        display(Markdown(f"## Clusters by resolution ({part + 1}/{CLUSTER_SLIDES})"))
        cluster_umap(s, part)

    for part in range(CLUSTER_SLIDES):
        display(Markdown(f"## Clusters in tissue by resolution ({part + 1}/{CLUSTER_SLIDES})"))
        spatial_sweep(s, part)

    display(Markdown("## Clusters in tissue"))
    spatial_clusters(s)
```
